client: I've been really stressed out lately about my final exams coming up next month, and honestly it's been keeping me up at night. Last term was rough — I struggled a lot with the coursework and felt like I was barely keeping my head above water, so now I'm terrified the same thing is going to happen again. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because at the end of the day I still have to sit down and actually pass these exams.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling this way — carrying the weight of last term's struggles while facing new exams is genuinely hard, and the sleep disruption only makes everything feel more overwhelming. You're also right that talking won't magically write the exams for you, but it can help us untangle some of the fear that might actually be getting in your way right now. I'm curious — when you imagine sitting down to study, what's the very first thought that tends to pop into your head?

client: Honestly, the first thought is usually something like "what's the point, you're going to blank out during the exam anyway." It's like my brain immediately jumps to the worst case scenario before I've even opened a textbook. And then I just kind of freeze up and end up scrolling on my phone instead of actually studying, which makes me feel even worse about myself afterward.
therapist: That thought — "what's the point, you're going to blank out anyway" — is a really clear example of your mind treating a fear as though it's already a fact, and it's no wonder it leads to freezing up, because who wants to invest effort in something they're convinced will fail? Then the scrolling brings temporary relief but leaves you with guilt, which actually feeds more evidence to that negative thought — it's a tough cycle. I'd love to gently challenge that original thought together: what actually happened in your exams last term — did you *completely* blank, or is your mind perhaps painting a darker picture than the full reality?

client: I mean, I didn't completely blank — I passed most of them, just not as well as I wanted to. But it honestly doesn't feel that different to me, because I know I should have done better and the grades I got aren't going to cut it if I want to stay in my program. So even when you put it that way, it's hard for me to feel like last term was anything other than a failure.
therapist: It's really important that you just acknowledged something significant — you *did* pass most of them, even while struggling, and that's real evidence that your brain doesn't simply blank out under pressure, even if it doesn't feel that way right now. The pain around not meeting your own standards is completely valid, and we don't need to dismiss that, but there's a difference between "I underperformed and need to adjust my approach" and "I'm going to fail" — one leaves room for change, the other just paralyzes you. What do you think might have actually gotten in the way of your performance last term — was it the studying itself, the anxiety, something else entirely?

client: Honestly, I think it was mostly the anxiety — I'd sit down to study and just spiral into worrying about how much I didn't know yet, and then hours would pass without me actually retaining anything. I also didn't really have anyone to study with or talk to about it, so it all just kind of built up inside my head with no outlet. I can see what you're saying about the difference between those two things, but I'm not sure how to actually feel that difference, you know? Like intellectually it makes sense, but emotionally it still feels like I'm heading toward the same wall.
therapist: That gap between knowing something intellectually and actually *feeling* it is one of the most honest and common experiences people have, and it doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong — it just means we need to find ways to build that felt sense gradually, through small experiences rather than just reframing thoughts. What's really striking me is that last term you were essentially fighting anxiety completely alone, with no outlet, and that isolation likely made the spiral so much worse than it needed to be. So I'm wondering — if we could identify just one small, concrete thing that might be different this term, whether that's a tiny study experiment or even just having this space to talk, what feels like it might actually be within reach for you?

client: I think having this space to talk is probably the most realistic thing right now, because the idea of joining a study group or reaching out to classmates feels pretty daunting when I barely know anyone in my program. But I guess I'm a little worried that just talking about it once a week isn't going to be enough to actually break the cycle when I'm sitting alone at my desk at 11pm and the spiral starts. Like, what am I supposed to do in that moment when there's no one around and my brain just goes into overdrive?
therapist: That's such a practical and self-aware question, and it tells me you're already thinking beyond our sessions toward actually breaking the cycle in real life — that matters. One thing we can work on together is building a kind of "in-the-moment toolkit" — for example, when the spiral starts, a simple grounding exercise or even writing down that "what's the point" thought and asking yourself one quick question like "is this a fact or a fear?" can create just enough distance to interrupt the autopilot. It won't feel natural at first, but the goal isn't to eliminate the anxiety instantly — it's to just slow it down enough that you can make a small choice, like opening one page, rather than reaching for your phone. When you imagine that 11pm moment, what do you think you'd need most — something to calm your body down, something to challenge the thought, or just a reminder that the spiral itself isn't the truth?

client: Probably a reminder that the spiral isn't the truth, because in those moments my body already feels so tense that trying to do a breathing exercise or write something down feels like way too many steps. But I'll be honest — I'm a little skeptical that just reminding myself "this is a fear, not a fact" is going to feel convincing when the anxiety is at its peak, because in that moment it genuinely feels like the truth. I guess I'm worried it'll just feel like I'm lying to myself rather than actually helping.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid — we're not aiming for you to convince yourself the anxiety is wrong in that peak moment, because that's actually really hard to do when your nervous system is in overdrive. Instead, the goal is something much smaller: not "this fear is definitely false" but rather "this feeling is intense *and* I've been here before and survived it" — it's less about winning an argument with your brain and more about just creating a tiny crack of doubt in the spiral's certainty. Given that you passed exams even while feeling this way last term, you actually have real evidence that the spiral has lied to you before — does that framing feel any different, or does it still feel like it wouldn't land in the moment?

client: That framing does feel a little different actually — "I've been here before and survived it" feels less like I'm trying to talk myself out of something and more like I'm just stating something that's already true. I think I could maybe hold onto that without it feeling fake. But I'm still a little nervous about whether I'll even remember to try it in the moment, because when the spiral hits it's like my whole brain just narrows and I forget everything except the panic.
therapist: I'm really glad that framing resonates — and the fact that it feels true rather than forced is actually what makes it more likely to work, because you're not fighting your brain, you're grounding it in reality. The forgetting-in-the-moment problem is so common and completely makes sense neurologically — panic genuinely narrows our thinking — which is why it can help to create a tiny external cue before the spiral hits, like a short phrase written on a sticky note at your desk or even as your phone wallpaper, so it's already in front of you when your brain can't retrieve it on its own. Would it feel manageable to try something like that this week — just choosing a spot where you usually spiral and placing one small reminder there — so we can see how it lands in a real moment?

client: A sticky note actually feels doable in a way that most things we've talked about haven't, so I'm not totally against trying it. I think my hesitation is more about what to actually write on it — like, I don't want it to become something I just stop seeing after a few days because it blends into the background. Is it okay if I figure out the exact wording between now and next session, or do you think I need to nail it down right now to actually follow through?
therapist: It's absolutely okay to figure out the wording on your own — in fact, the note will probably mean *more* to you if it comes from your own words rather than something I hand you, because your brain is more likely to actually "see" something that feels personally true. The one thing I'd gently suggest is giving yourself a specific moment to do it, like right after a meal or before bed one evening, rather than leaving it as an open "sometime this week" task, just so it doesn't quietly slip away. What do you think — is there a moment in the next day or two that feels realistic to sit down and try drafting it?

client: Tomorrow evening after dinner probably works, since that's usually when I'd otherwise just end up on my phone anyway. I guess my only worry is that I'll sit down to do it and then overthink every possible wording until I give up and tell myself I'll do it later. That's kind of a pattern for me — things that seem small still somehow turn into a big deal in my head.
therapist: It's really insightful that you can already see that pattern coming before it even happens — that kind of self-awareness is genuinely useful, and we can use it to set a small guardrail right now. What if you gave yourself a five-minute time limit and committed to whatever you've written by the end of it, even if it feels imperfect — because an imperfect sticky note on your desk tomorrow is worth infinitely more than a perfect one that never gets written? What's one version of the phrase, even rough and unpolished, that comes to mind right now?

client: Something like "you've felt this before and you got through it" is kind of coming to mind, which feels simple enough that I might actually write it without second-guessing it too much. I think the five-minute limit idea is smart because it removes the excuse to keep tinkering, though I'll be honest, part of me is already thinking I'll look at that note during a spiral and feel like it's too simple to actually help. I guess I just have to try it and see, which is kind of uncomfortable for me because I'd rather know it's going to work before I commit to it.
therapist: "You've felt this before and you got through it" is genuinely powerful — it's simple *because* it's true, and in a moment of panic, simple is exactly what your brain can actually absorb. And I want to gently reflect something back to you: that desire to know something will work before you try it is actually the same pattern that's been keeping you stuck at your desk — your brain wanting a guarantee before it's willing to invest, which is understandable but ultimately means nothing ever gets tested. What you just described — "I guess I just have to try it and see" — is actually a really courageous shift, so I'm curious, what would it mean for you if you tried it and it helped even just a little?
